title: Make sense of Live view
description: Choose useful live views and distinguish snapshot previews, full video and connection health.

chapters.title: A preview isn't a full live stream

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional operator opening Hub to check a loading bay. Several tiles are updating. Are they all sending the same kind of video?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Not necessarily. Preview uses a sequence of lightweight snapshots. Live uses a full video transport such as WebRTC or HLS, depending on deployment settings. Seeing a preview update is useful, but it doesn't prove that a full live session has connected.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes between those two live transports?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: WebRTC aims for low latency and supports compatible two-way audio. HLS delivers media over HTTPS with additional delay. Available choices depend on the configured services, feature flags, Agent capability and account plan.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Our operator has dozens of devices, but only needs the loading area. What's a sensible starting point?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use search, sites and status to narrow the grid. Then choose a layout that gives the relevant cameras enough space. Watching more streams isn't automatically better monitoring, especially on a browser already busy decoding video.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can administrators put boundaries on how many tiles appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Yes. The guide describes incremental loading, numbered pagination and a capped selection mode. Those are deployment choices. Select a manageable working set instead of expecting every connected camera to stream at full quality at once.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The loading-bay device looks online, but Talk isn't offered. Is that necessarily a broken stream?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Talk needs a compatible camera back-channel and the WebRTC live path. HLS doesn't supply that two-way audio channel. Controls also depend on device capability and permission, not only on whether a device is online.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And a motion badge isn't the same thing as video playback health?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. The device status, a recent event badge and the live stream's health answer different questions. A paused tile may simply be outside the viewport. Read the actual message before treating every placeholder as a camera failure.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where should the operator start if Live won't connect?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: First confirm the Agent is online and the account can access the device. Check Preview to establish whether snapshot delivery works, then investigate the live transport actually selected. WebRTC and HLS don't have the same network path.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So we shouldn't debug a WebRTC relay when the browser is really requesting an HLS playlist?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Right. Use the tile's health information and the guide's transport-specific checks. Narrow the view, distinguish status from stream health, and verify one working camera before expanding the grid. That's a much calmer start to a monitoring shift.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
